question: What is the main job of the glomerulus when making urine?

options.A: Reabsorbing essential glucose back into the bloodstream
options.B: Filtering water and small molecules from the blood
options.C: Secreting excess potassium directly into the tubules
options.D: Storing urine until it is ready for elimination

explanation: Think of the glomerulus like a high-pressure sieve! It pushes fluid and small waste products out of the blood and into the nephron so your body can start making urine. You've got this! [learn more](GNS123_U2_T6#GNS123_U2_T6_h1)

question: Why don't large proteins and blood cells normally show up in freshly filtered urine?

options.A: They are actively repelled by the urinary bladder walls
options.B: They are completely destroyed by enzymes in the glomerulus
options.C: They are immediately reabsorbed in the proximal tubule
options.D: They are too large to pass through the filtration membrane

explanation: Healthy kidney filters have tiny, careful pores. Blood cells and big proteins are simply too bulky to squeeze through, so they stay safely in the bloodstream where they belong! [learn more](GNS123_U2_T6#GNS123_U2_T6_h1)

question: Which urine collection method is best when a doctor suspects an infection and orders a urine culture?
explanation: The clean-catch midstream method is a classic! By letting the first bit of urine wash away skin germs, we catch a sample that truly shows what's happening inside the bladder. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T6#GNS123_U2_T6_h2)

question: A patient needs a very early pregnancy test using urine. Which sample should you tell her to collect?
explanation: First morning urine is the most concentrated, meaning any early pregnancy hormones will be nice and strong and easy for the test to pick up! [learn more](GNS123_U2_T6#GNS123_U2_T6_h2)

question: Finding protein in someone's routine urine test most often points to an issue with what?
explanation: Remember, healthy filters keep protein inside the blood. If protein is leaking into the urine, it's a good clue that the tiny filters in the kidneys might need some attention. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T6#GNS123_U2_T6_h3)

question: Why might a patient with poorly controlled diabetes have sugar (glucose) in their urine?

options.A: Kidney tubules stop functioning entirely due to excess insulin
options.B: High urinary pH converts normal proteins into simple sugar molecules
options.C: Blood sugar is so high it overwhelms kidney reabsorption capacity
options.D: The pancreas secretes extra glucose directly into the bladder

explanation: Normally, the kidneys rescue and reabsorb all the sugar. But when blood sugar is super high, the little kidney tubules get overworked and the extra sugar spills over into the urine! [learn more](GNS123_U2_T6#GNS123_U2_T6_h3)

question: Which lab finding under a microscope points strongly to a kidney infection (pyelonephritis) rather than a simple bladder infection?
explanation: Casts are tiny mold-shaped clumps that form way up inside the kidney tubes. Finding white cell casts tells us the infection has traveled high up into the kidneys! [learn more](GNS123_U2_T6#GNS123_U2_T6_h4)

question: What is the main reason lab technicians spin urine in a machine (centrifuge) before looking at it under a microscope?

options.A: To kill any live bacteria that might distort the viewing field
options.B: To concentrate solid particles at the bottom into a sediment pellet
options.C: To break down large protein strands that block the microscope lens
options.D: To raise the temperature of the sample for better chemical reactivity

explanation: Centrifuging acts like a quick spin cycle that gathers all the heavy cells, crystals, and casts neatly at the bottom of the tube so they are super easy to spot and study. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T6#GNS123_U2_T6_h4)

question: What is the main goal of the 'sensitivity' part of a urine culture and sensitivity (C&S) test?

options.A: To determine which antibiotics will kill the specific bacteria
options.B: To measure the exact volume of urine produced in 24 hours
options.C: To calculate the patient's specific gravity and hydration status
options.D: To check if red blood cells are fragile under chemical stress

explanation: The sensitivity test is like a test-run for medicines! It shows us which exact antibiotic will successfully knock out the patient's specific infection. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T6#GNS123_U2_T6_h5)

question: A patient asks why their urine culture takes up to 48 hours while a dipstick takes minutes. What is the best way to explain this?

options.A: The chemical strips must be shipped to a centralized government lab
options.B: Microscopic slides take longer to dry under special laboratory lamps
options.C: Bacteria need time to multiply in the lab before they can be identified
options.D: Hospital policy requires waiting two days to ensure billing is complete

explanation: Good things take time! Bacteria are tiny living things that need a little time to grow and form visible colonies on a lab plate before we can figure out what they are. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T6#GNS123_U2_T6_h5)

question: What action officially marks the start time of a 24-hour urine collection test?

options.A: Having the patient empty their bladder and discarding that urine
options.B: Drinking two large glasses of water right before the test starts
options.C: Saving the very first morning urine sample in the collection jug
options.D: Collecting all urine produced starting from midnight regardless of sleep

explanation: To get an accurate 24-hour count, we start with a totally empty bladder so we don't accidentally count old urine that sat in the body overnight! [learn more](GNS123_U2_T6#GNS123_U2_T6_h6)

question: A patient doing a 24-hour urine collection tells you they accidentally flushed one sample halfway through the day. What should you do?

options.A: Discard the current collection and restart the entire 24-hour process
options.B: Estimate the missed amount and add extra water to make up the volume
options.C: Extend the collection period by twelve hours to make up for the loss
options.D: Send the incomplete jug to the lab with a note explaining the lost sample

explanation: Ah, frustration! But a 24-hour test has to be complete. Missing even one bathroom trip means the numbers won't be accurate, so it's best to start fresh another day. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T6#GNS123_U2_T6_h6)

question: Why is it so important to send a routine urine sample to the lab right away, or keep it in the fridge if there's a delay?

options.A: Prompt delivery prevents the patient from changing their mind about the test
options.B: Room temperature encourages bacterial growth and chemical breakdown
options.C: Leaving it out causes the plastic container to melt in warm rooms
options.D: Refrigeration speeds up the chemical reaction on dipstick pads

explanation: Urine left sitting in a warm room changes quickly—bacteria love to multiply in it, and cellular casts start to break apart, which ruins the accuracy of the test! [learn more](GNS123_U2_T6#GNS123_U2_T6_h7)

question: What is an essential safety action you must take immediately before collecting any urine specimen from a patient?

options.A: Verifying the patient's identity using two identifiers
options.B: Warming the collection cup to body temperature in warm water
options.C: Administering a prophylactic dose of broad-spectrum antibiotics
options.D: Requesting a formal psychiatric evaluation for anxiety

explanation: Safety first, always! Always double-check who your patient is using two unique markers (like their name and hospital number) before doing any clinical procedure. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T6#GNS123_U2_T6_h7)
